title_en: James Bosworth on What Comes After Lula's Stunning Win
title_zh: James Bosworth 谈 Lula 惊艳胜选之后的巴西与拉美
subtitle_zh: Lula 逆转 Bolsonaro 胜选背后：反现任浪潮、福音派崛起与委内瑞拉变局。
description: James Bosworth on What Comes After Lula's Stunning Win

turns.en: Hey there, Odd Lots listeners. Tracy Alloway here.
turns.zh: 嗨，Odd Lots 的听众们，我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: And Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: We have had an absolutely amazing year, and we've gotten to see some of our listeners, meet some of our listeners across the country at some of our live shows. But we are very excited because we are coming back home to NYC for another live recording.
turns.zh: 这一年我们过得太精彩了，在全国各地的现场演出里，我们见到了一些听众、也认识了一些听众。但我们特别兴奋，因为我们要回到大本营 NYC，再做一场现场录制。

turns.en: We have a really exciting lineup of perfect guests, including Lena Kahn, Pablo Torre, and Adam Tooze. And we really hope to see you there.
turns.zh: 我们有一阵容特别棒、堪称完美的嘉宾，包括 Lena Kahn、Pablo Torre 和 Adam Tooze。我们真心希望能在现场见到你们。

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: So join us on December 9th at City Winery for another live taping of the Oddlots podcast. Tickets are now on sale at Bloomberg.com forward slash Oddlots.
turns.zh: 所以请在 12 月 9 日到 City Winery 加入我们，一起来看 Oddlots 播客的又一场现场录制。门票现已开售，地址是 Bloomberg.com 斜杠 Oddlots。

turns.en: Or check the show notes here for a direct link. And either way, hope to see you there. Podcasts, radio, news. Hello and welcome to another episode of the Odd Lots Podcast. I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 或者在这里的节目备注（show notes）里找直接链接。不管怎样，希望能见到你们。播客、广播、新闻。大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots Podcast。我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: And I'm Tracy Alloway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: So we're recording this on November 3rd, Election Day in the U.S., But there's really much to talk about during the election day itself. Everyone's just waiting.
turns.zh: 我们这期是在 11 月 3 日录的，也就是美国的选举日（Election Day）。不过选举日当天其实没什么太多可聊的，大家都在等结果。

turns.en: It's a bit of an anti-climax, isn't it? You wait for election day and then like nothing really happens.
turns.zh: 这有点反高潮（anti-climax），是吧？你一直等着选举日，结果当天其实什么都没发生。

turns.en: Something might happen. But yeah, nothing happens during the day. So the day of election day is actually a really good time to talk about a bunch of other stuff. Talk about other elections. Yeah, to talk about other things that are going on because nothing really happens that day. But we did recently have other elections, as you hinted at, in Brazil.
turns.zh: 也许会发生点什么吧。但 yeah，当天确实什么都没发生。所以选举日当天其实是聊一堆别的事情的好时机。聊聊别的选举。Yeah，聊聊其他正在发生的事，因为那天本身没什么可说的。不过就像你暗示的，我们最近确实在巴西经历了另一场选举。

turns.en: That's right. So we had a very, very surprise victory by Lula over Flavio Bolsonaro. And then Flavio Bolsonaro escaped Brazil. He fled, yeah. So that's a really interesting question, like what that means for Brazil-U.S. relations. The other thing that's been happening is Venezuela, right?
turns.zh: 没错。Lula 出人意料地击败了 Flavio Bolsonaro，赢得非常、非常意外。然后 Flavio Bolsonaro 逃离了巴西。他跑路了，yeah。所以就出现了一个很有意思的问题：这对巴西和美国的关系意味着什么。另一件一直在发生的事是委内瑞拉（Venezuela），对吧？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: Yeah。

turns.en: So right before we came on this podcast, there was a headline out of the New York Times saying that the U.S. was in discussions to set up a military presence in Venezuela.
turns.zh: 就在我们上这期播客之前，New York Times 出了一条头条，说美国正在讨论在委内瑞拉设立军事存在（military presence）。

turns.en: Oh, interesting.
turns.zh: 哦，有意思。

turns.en: So, you know, that raises questions as well over whether or not like Venezuela is basically becoming a protectorate of the U.S., I guess. Right.
turns.zh: 所以你看，这也引出了疑问：委内瑞拉是不是基本上正在变成美国的一个保护国（protectorate），我想。对吧。

turns.en: So one of the things that we know is that the Trump administration, or at least the State Department, has this sort of weird, maybe surprisingly friendly relations with Delce Rodriguez, the successor to Maduro, who we captured and now have in custody in New York earlier this year. And so, but like recently, like there's been the return of the Democratic challenger there.
turns.zh: 我们已经知道的一点是，Trump 政府、或者至少国务院（State Department），跟 Delcy Rodriguez 之间有一种挺奇怪、甚至可以说是意外友好的关系。Delcy Rodriguez 是 Maduro 的继任者——Maduro 今年早些时候被我们抓获，现在关押在纽约。不过最近，那边的民主党挑战者又回来了。

turns.en: The opposition leader.
turns.zh: 那位反对派领袖。

turns.en: The opposition leader, et cetera. So it's sort of an interesting time to like catch up. Did we use this time?
turns.zh: 对，那位反对派领袖，等等。所以现在是补上这些进展的一个挺有意思的时机。那我们就趁这个机会聊聊吧？

turns.en: Let's talk about other American elections. Let's talk about other- South American elections.
turns.zh: 我们来聊聊其他的美国选举吧。我们来聊聊其他的——南美洲的选举吧。

turns.en: Politics elsewhere in the hemisphere. Anyway, very excited to have back on the podcast. We talked to him earlier this year. James Bosworth, he's non-resident fellow at the Stimson Center and he is the author of the excellent newsletter- the Latin America Risk Report. James, thanks so much for coming back on Odd Lots.
turns.zh: 聊聊这个半球其他地方的政治。总之，非常高兴能请他再次回到我们的播客，今年早些时候我们跟他聊过。James Bosworth，他是 Stimson Center 的非驻地研究员（non-resident fellow），也是那份出色通讯（newsletter）——Latin America Risk Report 的作者。James，非常感谢你再次来到 Odd Lots。

turns.en: Thank you for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们邀请我。

turns.en: Just tell us, how did Lula win after even going into that day, all the math and polls and everything thought it was pretty clearly going to be Flavio Bolsonaro?
turns.zh: 就跟我们说说吧，进入到投票日那天，所有的测算、民调等等都相当明确地认为会是 Flavio Bolsonaro 胜出，Lula 到底是怎么赢的？

turns.en: So there are two answers to that. One is that Flavio was a terrible candidate, and the other was that Lula was a great candidate. So let me run through those both, right? Flavio was a terrible candidate. In fact, when I was here in New York the last time, I gave a presentation elsewhere and someone asked, what could Flavio Bolsonaro do better? And I said, change his last name. There's an element in which being a Bolsonaro was a weight on him. And I mean, you go back and his father, Jair Bolsonaro, former president, was accused of, convicted of being involved in a coup attempt in 2022, 2023. And if you remember January 8th, 2023, very similar to January 6th, 2021, there was a big event in Brasilia where a mob of protesters took over various buildings in the capital. And so Jair Bolsonaro was convicted of that. But Flavio has had issues. Five years ago, he was accused of money laundering while he was a congressman. Earlier this year, he was connected to Daniel Vocaro, who was the head of Banco Master, which was a big financial scandal in Brazil, and was caught on WhatsApp asking for millions of dollars from this banker.
turns.zh: 对此有两个答案。一是 Flavio 是个糟糕透顶的候选人，二是 Lula 是个极其出色的候选人。我两个都讲一遍，好吗？Flavio 是个很差的候选人。事实上，我上次来纽约的时候，在别处做了一场演讲，有人问，Flavio Bolsonaro 能怎么做得更好？我说，改了他的姓。在某种意义上，姓 Bolsonaro 对他是一种拖累。你回想一下，他父亲、前总统 Jair Bolsonaro 被指控、并被定罪参与了 2022、2023 年的一场未遂政变。如果你记得 2023 年 1 月 8 日——跟 2021 年 1 月 6 日非常相似——在巴西利亚（Brasilia）发生了一起大事件，一群抗议者占领了首都的多座建筑。Jair Bolsonaro 就是因为这件事被定罪的。而 Flavio 自己也有一堆问题。五年前，他在担任国会议员期间被指控洗钱（money laundering）。今年早些时候，他又跟 Daniel Vocaro 扯上了关系——此人是 Banco Master 的负责人，那是一桩巴西的大金融丑闻——而且他被抓到在 WhatsApp 上向这位银行家索要数百万美元。

turns.en: Seems bad.
turns.zh: 听起来很糟糕。

turns.en: It was bad. Right before the election, there was a Brazilian magazine that tied him to pharmaceutical lobbyists and prostitutes on a boat. And then even when he fled from Brazil, the plane he flew from Argentina to the US on was connected to a money laundering investigation inside of Argentina and a drug trafficking case in Texas.
turns.zh: 确实很糟。就在选举前，有一家巴西杂志把他跟一艘船上的医药说客和妓女联系在了一起。而且即便在他逃离巴西的时候，他从阿根廷飞往美国所乘的那架飞机，也跟阿根廷境内的一起洗钱调查以及得克萨斯州（Texas）的一桩毒品贩运案有关联。

turns.en: I want to get into all these details, but just All of this was true prior to the first round of the voting, right? So all of these negatives on him were in the case when he came in first during the first round of voting. So where did something go change or what was the mechanism via which that didn't translate to the final round?
turns.zh: 我想深挖所有这些细节，但先说一句：所有这些事在第一轮投票之前就已经是事实了，对吧？也就是说，在他第一轮投票中拔得头筹的时候，这些负面消息就已经都存在了。那么，到底是什么地方变了，或者说是什么样的机制，让第一轮的领先没能延续到最终一轮？

turns.en: Across the last six years, eight years in Latin America, really across much of the world, we've been in an anti-incumbent environment. Everything is a referendum on the incumbent. And Lula da Silva was sitting at 45% in the polls. And the first round was really a referendum on Lula. It wasn't about Flavio Bolsonaro. In some ways, coming in first place in the first round was the worst thing that could happen to Flavio Bolsonaro because all of a sudden, all of the attention got put on him and it let Lula catch up from behind. It shook up his campaign and gave him the opportunity to win.
turns.zh: 在过去六到八年里，在拉美、其实在全球大部分地区，我们都处在一个反现任（anti-incumbent）的环境里。凡事都变成对现任者的一场公投。而 Lula da Silva 当时在民调里停在 45%。第一轮其实是对 Lula 的公投，跟 Flavio Bolsonaro 没什么关系。某种意义上，第一轮拿到第一名，反而是发生在 Flavio Bolsonaro 身上最糟糕的事，因为突然间所有的注意力都集中到了他身上，这让 Lula 得以从后面追上来。它打乱了 Lula 的竞选节奏，也给了他赢的机会。

turns.en: Didn't he shake up his campaign strategy as well? I heard he hired a social media manager, put Put younger people in charge of some of it. The WhatsApp group.
turns.zh: 他不是也调整了自己的竞选策略吗？我听说他请了一位社交媒体经理，让一些更年轻的人来负责其中一部分。就是那个 WhatsApp 群。

turns.en: He got his first cell phone. Lula had never had a smartphone before. Yes, they started Lula's Army, a WhatsApp group that had, I think, over 10 million people on it. Over 5% of Brazilian voters were on this WhatsApp group. And the day of the election, when there were various shenanigans on both sides, everybody plays dirty tricks, but certain mayors blocked the bus service. The WhatsApp group got into mode and started driving voters to the polls. Things like that really mattered. And Lula, who had never really understood social media, even though Brazil is the most online country potentially in the entire world, Lula had really, he nailed it during the debates. He hit these little 30-second clips that were perfect to share on social media. I don't know if he did it intentionally or not, but it was perfect.
turns.zh: 他有了人生第一部手机。Lula 以前从来没用过智能手机。是的，他们搞了个叫 Lula's Army 的 WhatsApp 群，我记得上面有超过 1000 万人。超过 5% 的巴西选民都在这个 WhatsApp 群里。选举日那天，双方都有各种小动作——每个人都会玩脏招——但有些市长把公交服务给停了。这个 WhatsApp 群立刻进入状态，开始开车把选民送到投票站。这类事情真的很关键。而 Lula，尽管巴西可能是全世界最'在线'的国家，他却从来没真正搞懂过社交媒体，可这回他在辩论中的表现堪称完美。他抛出了那些 30 秒的小片段，特别适合在社交媒体上转发。我不知道他是不是有意为之，但效果堪称完美。

turns.en: Some people just have that. You know, it's interesting what you say about this sort of like anti-incumbent bias working against Bolsonaro due to him having won the first round. I saw some people speculate, you know, in Universe B, where the U.S. is a different electoral system, whether Trump would have won in 2016 or had the first round been like, okay, let's narrow it down to the final two, kick off all the random third parties. Like, oh, like it's going to be Trump. Like, maybe not. You know, it's like, you never really know. But I could, I sort of get that, what you're saying. Like, it's sort of like resetting the expectations of who the president is. Right.
turns.zh: 有些人就是天生有这种本事。你知道，你说到因为 Bolsonaro 赢了第一轮、反而让这种反现任偏差对他不利，这一点很有意思。我看到有人推测，在一个'平行宇宙 B'里，如果美国是另一种选举制度，Trump 在 2016 年还会不会赢；或者如果第一轮是那种'好，我们把范围缩小到最后两名，把所有乱七八糟的第三方都踢出去'的模式，那结果会怎样。就像，哦，那肯定就是 Trump 了。也可能不是。你知道，这种事你真的说不准。但我大致能明白你的意思，就像是在重新设定大家对'谁会当总统'的预期。对吧。

turns.en: I mean, usually across two round elections, usually the first round winner wins. But occasionally, I mean, the reason you have the second round is so these things can happen. So voters can have that moment. And so the president can build a potential majority coalition for themselves.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，在两轮选举里，通常第一轮的赢家最终会赢。但偶尔也会有例外——毕竟设第二轮的意义，就是为了让这种事情有可能发生，让选民有那么一个重新选择的时刻，也让当选者能为自己搭建一个潜在的多数联盟（majority coalition）。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: Yeah。

turns.en: Correct me if I'm wrong, but didn't you have a Bolsonaro win as your base case?
turns.zh: 如果我说错了请纠正我，但你之前不是把 Bolsonaro 胜选当作你的基准情形（base case）吗？

turns.en: So I had Bolsonaro winning. The night before the election, I had Bolsonaro winning at about 64%. So prior to the first round, I was essentially coin flip.
turns.zh: 对，我原本判断 Bolsonaro 会赢。选举前一晚，我给 Bolsonaro 的胜率是大约 64%。而在第一轮之前，我基本上认为是五五开（coin flip）。

turns.en: You thought it was 64% chance to win, not 64%.
turns.zh: 你说的是 64% 的获胜概率，不是 64%（的得票率）。

turns.en: To win, yes, yes. Exactly. 64% chance to win. And the prediction markets were at 80%. Yeah, they were. In fact, there was a moment where the prediction markets hit 87% for Bolsonaro. And so there's always this element of who got it less wrong becomes a real question in some of these prediction market things. And I know that this was a big miss for the prediction markets, right? I mean, you always wonder, was this the 20% shot that happened or did they miss? I will tell you, they missed. They were overconfident on this election. I missed. I wish I had been lower on the floppy odds.
turns.zh: 获胜概率，是的，没错，正是如此。64% 的获胜概率。而预测市场（prediction markets）当时给到了 80%。是的，确实如此。事实上有一阵子，预测市场对 Bolsonaro 的概率一度冲到 87%。所以在这些预测市场的事情上，总有一个问题：到底是谁错得没那么离谱。我知道这次对预测市场来说是个大大的失手，对吧？你总会想，这到底是那 20% 的小概率真的发生了，还是他们判断错了？我可以告诉你，他们是判断错了。他们在这场选举上过于自信了。我也错了，我真希望当时把 Flavio 的胜算压得更低一些。

turns.en: But you obviously thought that Lula had a real chance of winning.
turns.zh: 但你显然认为 Lula 是有实打实的获胜机会的。

turns.en: Oh, absolutely. You know, better than a third, right? They had a chance of winning. And the reasons were, I mean, you could see him slowly catching up in the polls and you could see his campaign just doing well, generally. Now, I can't base a prediction on vibes. All of the data, all of the polls said Flavio Bolsonaro was going to win. And so, I mean, based on the first in the first round data, it looked like Flavio winning. But, you know, you have to sort of factor in, OK, but he's catching up and the polls seem to be hurting together and correlated. And there were other issues as well. So that all went.
turns.zh: 哦，那是当然。你知道，比三分之一还高，对吧？他是有机会赢的。原因是，你能看到他在民调里慢慢追上来，也能看到他的竞选整体上做得很好。当然，我不能光凭感觉（vibes）来做预测。所有的数据、所有的民调都说 Flavio Bolsonaro 会赢。所以基于第一轮的数据看，当时像是 Flavio 要赢。但你知道，你又得把一些因素考虑进去：好，他在追赶，而且各项民调似乎都在朝一起靠拢、彼此相关联。此外还有别的问题。所以这些都……

turns.en: Into the model. How much of the miss by prediction markets and pollsters, I guess, had to do with, I guess, surprise voters actually turning out in the election? Because it seems like maybe a lot of people who weren't polled actually turned up and voted for Lula.
turns.zh: 纳入了模型。那么，预测市场和民调机构这次的失手，有多少跟意外冒出来投票的选民有关？因为看起来，也许有很多没被民调覆盖到的人真的现身、投了 Lula。

turns.en: So on one hand, it's really small numbers. The change in turnout from the first round to the second round was less than 2%. You had a slight shift in terms of non-voters, people who cast blank or invalidated ballots the first round. You had another 1% or 2%. But in Brazil, that's a couple million votes. And in an election won by 4 million votes, you know, a shift of 1% or 2% across those rounds really did make the difference.
turns.zh: 一方面，这些数字其实很小。从第一轮到第二轮，投票率（turnout）的变化不到 2%。此外在没投票的人、以及第一轮投了空白票或废票的人当中，也有轻微的转移，又有 1% 到 2%。但在巴西，那就是好几百万张选票。而在一场以 400 万票差距赢下的选举里，你知道，两轮之间 1% 到 2% 的这种转移，真的就决定了结果。

turns.en: Wait, what's the deal with Bolsonaro's stepmom?
turns.zh: 等等，Bolsonaro 的继母是怎么回事？

turns.en: Michelle?
turns.zh: Michelle？

turns.en: Yeah. What was the deal? I saw in your newsletter, you mentioned something she said or did that didn't help the race. What was that all about?
turns.zh: 对。怎么回事？我在你的 newsletter 里看到，你提到她说了或做了什么，对竞选不利。那到底是怎么回事？

turns.en: So early on, Michelle, who's a stepmom, Michelle Bolsonaro had, and she won a Senate seat, by the way, during this past election. Oh, good for her. But she and Flavio had a little fight and then they made up. And now she's considering changing parties potentially, which is also odd to leave the Bolsonaro party when her last name is Bolsonaro. But she and Flavio had this just spat in which it seemed like Flavio was not respecting her. And because Flavio... was already weak among women voters, this did not help the odds for his campaign. Across the whole campaign, he had setback after setback. It's actually impressive. He did as well as he did in the first round. But his campaign, he was also very professional. If you watched him in the debates, he was very well coached. He didn't answer the questions, but that's typical in a lot of debates across democracies. He was very well coached. He did not do poorly in the debates.
turns.zh: 事情是这样的，早先 Michelle——就是那位继母 Michelle Bolsonaro——顺便说一句，她在这次选举里还赢下了一个参议院席位。哦，那挺为她高兴的。但她和 Flavio 闹过一点小矛盾，后来又和好了。现在她又在考虑可能要换个党，这也挺奇怪的，毕竟她姓 Bolsonaro，却要离开 Bolsonaro 所在的党。她和 Flavio 有过这么一次口角，看起来 Flavio 不太尊重她。而因为 Flavio 本来在女性选民中就比较弱势，这就对他的竞选胜算没什么帮助。纵观整场竞选，他一个挫折接一个挫折。说实话，他在第一轮能表现得这么好，已经挺让人佩服的了。不过他的竞选团队也很专业。如果你看他在辩论里的表现，他受到了很好的调教。他不回答问题，但这在很多民主国家的辩论里都是常态。他被训练得很好，在辩论里表现得并不差。

turns.en: Well, speaking of Bolsonaro's party, are you seeing like a fracturing there? Because I think he's rejecting the results of the election from the US where he now is. But meanwhile, his party has accepted the result, right? So like, His own party has accepted the result that he's rejecting. What does that mean?
turns.zh: 那么，说到 Bolsonaro 的政党，你有没有看到那里出现分裂（fracturing）？因为我觉得他现在人在美国，正从那边拒绝承认选举结果。但与此同时，他的党却接受了这个结果，对吧？也就是说，他自己的党接受了他所拒绝的结果。这意味着什么？

turns.en: The fracturing is not as bad as it was four years ago. I mean, four years ago, after Jair's attempted coup, there was a real fracture. And you saw a lot of centrist parties jump in and support Lula. It gave Lula big support for the first year of his presidency in this most recent term. This time, you do see it's not a fracturing, but it's a recognition, I think, that maybe the Bolsonaros shouldn't be the candidates in 2030, right? They're already playing this out and saying, we need to figure out a strategy because everybody knows that if the candidate had been Tarcísio de Freitas, who won the governor of Sao Paulo or any other right-wing candidate, they would have, that person would have defeated Lula. I feel convinced of it. Every Brazilian analyst feels convinced of it. So the question is, how do we avoid running the Bolsonaros in 2030 so that somebody else can run because that candidate will be a stronger candidate than anyone with the last name of Bolsonaro?
turns.zh: 这次的分裂没有四年前那么严重。四年前，在 Jair 未遂政变之后，确实出现了真正的破裂，你能看到很多中间派政党跳出来支持 Lula。这在 Lula 最近这个任期的头一年里给了他很大的支持。而这一次，你看到的其实不是分裂，而是一种认知，我觉得：也许 Bolsonaro 家的人不该在 2030 年出来当候选人，对吧？他们已经在盘算这件事，说我们需要想清楚一个策略，因为大家都清楚，如果当时的候选人是 Tarcísio de Freitas——他赢得了圣保罗（Sao Paulo）州长——或者任何一个其他右翼候选人，那个人本来是会击败 Lula 的。我对此深信不疑，每一个巴西分析师都深信不疑。所以问题就变成了：我们要怎么避免在 2030 年再让 Bolsonaro 家的人出来选，好让别人能出来参选，因为那样的人选会比任何姓 Bolsonaro 的人更有竞争力？

turns.en: I have a question, and this is something I know nothing about. It's not even really related to the election specifically. In fact, it's one of those things you read an article about every once in a while and forget. After Brazil, they did badly in the World Cup this year, and I saw a bunch of people on social media complaining or tweeting, like, oh, Brazil hasn't been good at soccer ever since the Catholic population of the country has declined. these evangelicals can't play soccer. This is just tweets that I saw. Can you talk a little bit about the sort of like politics and the rise, like the historical rise? I mostly associate Latin American countries with Catholicism, but I know these are like dated takes and that across Latin America, there's been a pretty big rise in like American style, evangelical Christianity, et cetera. Can you talk a little bit about who that demographic is? is like that shift, that wave, et cetera.
turns.zh: 我有个问题，这方面我完全不懂。它其实跟这次选举也没什么直接关系。事实上，它属于那种你偶尔读到一篇文章、然后就忘了的话题。今年巴西在世界杯（World Cup）上表现很差，之后我看到一堆人在社交媒体上抱怨或者发推说，哦，自从巴西的天主教人口下降以来，巴西足球就一直不行了；这些福音派（evangelicals）不会踢球。这只是我看到的推文。你能不能稍微谈谈这背后的政治，以及这种历史性的崛起？我大体上会把拉美国家和天主教（Catholicism）联系在一起，但我知道这些都是过时的看法了，而且在整个拉美，美式福音派基督教（evangelical Christianity）之类的兴起相当明显。你能不能谈谈这个群体到底是谁？就是这种转变、这股浪潮等等。

turns.en: And it's hard because the evangelicals also correlate somewhat more with rural voters in certain areas. The urban voters, as occurs in the United States in some ways. Right. But the evangelical rise in Brazil has definitely created a divide inside of the electorate. And you saw it every poll. There's not really exit polls in the same way we have in the U.S., but every poll in Brazil showed that the evangelical community largely voted for Bolsonaro and the Catholic community largely voted for Lula. But as evangelicals and Catholics are getting closer, close to parity in Brazil.
turns.zh: 这事儿挺难说的，因为在某些地区，福音派信徒更多地跟农村选民相关联——而不是城市选民，这一点在某种程度上跟美国的情况一样。对吧。但巴西福音派的崛起，确实在选民内部造成了一道裂痕。你在每一份民调里都能看到这个。巴西并没有像我们美国那样的出口民调（exit polls），但巴西的每一份民调都显示，福音派群体大体上投给了 Bolsonaro，而天主教群体大体上投给了 Lula。而随着福音派和天主教信徒在巴西的人数越来越接近、几乎持平……

turns.en: What has driven that, though? What is the long-term structural driver of the growth of evangelical Christianity across Latin America?
turns.zh: 不过，是什么在推动这一点呢？在整个拉美，福音派基督教增长的长期结构性驱动因素是什么？

turns.en: To self-define, they're evangelical. They are constantly recruiting. They're self-promoters, Joe. And the Catholic Church, I think, has fallen behind on certain aspects of that. I think the other aspect of this is, there's elements of the Catholic Church, in the United States and in Latin America that are quite conservative, small C conservative in terms of how they view social policy. And Lula's coalition is much more small L liberal in the sense of they will support gay marriage. And I think that divide has caused the Catholic Church to have some drop in Latin America and in Brazil while the evangelical community has taken advantage of that.
turns.zh: 从自我界定（self-define）来说，他们就是福音派。他们在不断地招募信众。他们是自我推销者，Joe。而我认为，天主教会（Catholic Church）在这方面已经落后了。我觉得另一个方面是，在美国和拉美，天主教会内部有一些部分相当保守——是那种在社会政策上'小 c'的保守（conservative）。而 Lula 的联盟则更像是'小 l'的自由派（liberal），也就是他们会支持同性婚姻。我认为正是这道分歧，导致天主教会在拉美和巴西有所衰落，而福音派群体则趁机占了便宜。

turns.en: The last time we had you on this podcast, you talked about an orange wave or the idea of a bunch of Latin American leaders sort of aligning themselves with Trump and striking deals and all of that. With the surprise result in Brazil, does that mean that the orange wave has crested, I guess, or is Brazil an exception?
turns.zh: 上一次请你上我们播客的时候，你谈到了'橙色浪潮'（orange wave），也就是一批拉美领导人向 Trump 靠拢、跟他达成各种协议之类的这个说法。那么巴西这个出人意料的结果，是不是意味着这股橙色浪潮已经到顶了，还是说巴西只是个例外？

turns.en: It's a great question. Everyone's watching Argentina next year to find out what the answer to that is. So there's sort of two questions here, right? One is this idea that there are a bunch of pro-Trump leaders who have won. And whether that was because there's been a shift to the right or just a pendulum in an anti-incumbent environment, I tend to be the latter explanation. Trump was going around saying he was nine for nine in elections recently. He just pulled that number out.
turns.zh: 这是个很好的问题。明年所有人都会盯着阿根廷，来看这个问题的答案。这里其实有两个问题，对吧？一个是这种说法：有一批亲 Trump 的领导人胜选了。而这究竟是因为出现了向右的转变，还是只是在反现任环境里的一次钟摆效应——我更倾向于后一种解释。Trump 到处说他最近在选举里'九战九胜'，那个数字是他随口编出来的。

turns.en: Of the air.
turns.zh: 凭空编出来的。

turns.en: But it's relatively close to how he had done prior to Brazil. There's still going to be for the next two years an orange shift in the sense that you have this element of Every Latin American leader, right, left, center, must respond to Trump. He forces them to respond, right? So even though Lula has won this election and the election did not go Trump's way and Trump is now trying to back away a bit from Bolsonaro, you have Lula to Silva having to work with Trump, having to respond to Trump, having to deal with tariffs. You have Claudia Scheinbaum in Mexico having to do the same. Everyone has to respond to Trump, whether or not they agree with him. And that's still going to define the following two years until Trump leaves office in January, 2029.
turns.zh: 但这也跟他此前的表现相差不大，跟巴西之前的情况挺接近。未来两年仍然会有一场'橙色转变'，意思是说，有这么一个因素：每一位拉美领导人——不管右、左还是中间——都必须回应 Trump。他逼着他们去回应，对吧？所以尽管 Lula 赢下了这场选举、结果并不如 Trump 所愿，而且 Trump 现在正试图跟 Bolsonaro 稍微拉开点距离，可 Lula da Silva 还是不得不跟 Trump 打交道、不得不回应 Trump、不得不应对关税（tariffs）。墨西哥的 Claudia Scheinbaum 也一样得这么做。每个人都必须回应 Trump，无论他们是否认同他。这一点仍将定义接下来的两年，直到 Trump 在 2029 年 1 月卸任。

turns.en: How much has the Iran war specifically flipped the sign, so to speak, about the value of being good friends with Trump in Latin America?
turns.zh: 具体到伊朗战争（Iran war），它在多大程度上——可以说是——扭转了在拉美跟 Trump 做好朋友这件事的价值正负号？

turns.en: So it really hasn't impacted– Latin American leaders are not responding to Trump's Iran war directly.
turns.zh: 其实它并没有产生什么影响——拉美领导人并没有直接对 Trump 的伊朗战争做出回应。

turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯哼。

turns.en: At the same time, the Iran war has driven up oil prices and fuel costs around the region, which is just bad for incumbents generally.
turns.zh: 但与此同时，伊朗战争推高了整个地区的油价和燃料成本，而这一般来说对现任者都是不利的。

turns.en: Oh, I see.
turns.zh: 哦，我明白了。

turns.en: When you have higher fuel costs or higher inflation in Latin America, every incumbent is going to suffer. And that's what you've seen in Chile and Colombia and Peru.
turns.zh: 当拉美出现更高的燃料成本或更高的通胀（inflation）时，每一个现任者都会遭殃。这就是你在智利（Chile）、哥伦比亚（Colombia）和秘鲁（Peru）看到的情况。

turns.en: But it's just inflation. There's not... Because you don't think it goes a little bit further where it's like, yeah, here's this guy that you went to the White House and you were buddy-buddy with him. And this war that he started... which almost no one around the world except for the United States and Israel really care about, has caused inflation to get to rise. That hasn't created a political penalty, in your view, for politicians who made the choice to be friends with Trump?
turns.zh: 但这只是通胀而已。并没有……因为你不觉得事情会再往前推一步，变成这样：喏，就是那个你跑去白宫、跟他称兄道弟的家伙，他挑起的这场战争——除了美国和以色列，世界上几乎没人真正在乎——导致了通胀上升。在你看来，这并没有给那些选择跟 Trump 做朋友的政治人物带来政治上的代价吗？

turns.en: It doesn't seem to have mattered in any of the polls I have seen. What you do see are people are angry at inflation. But people aren't making the big logical leap necessarily. But all elections are local and local incumbents get blamed for inflation. Therefore, higher gas prices whether it's caused by the Iran war or something else, get blamed on the incumbent. Now, one interesting twist for Brazil, Brazil is very much in commodity exporting economy. If there have been higher commodity prices over the last six months, they're exporting oil, they're exporting soy. They have benefited in some ways from the Iran war. I mean, certainly the Caribbean and Central America have been hit hard. Brazil, it's sort of net effect is sort of a wash actually. And that may have helped Lula, though it's going to be a long time until we really are able to look at the data to understand that.
turns.zh: 在我看到的任何民调里，这似乎都不重要。你确实能看到的是，民众对通胀感到愤怒。但人们未必会做出那一大步的逻辑跳跃。不过所有选举都是地方性的，本地的现任者会因为通胀而被责怪。因此，更高的油价——不管是由伊朗战争还是别的原因造成的——都会被算到现任者头上。现在，对巴西来说有个有意思的转折：巴西在很大程度上是一个大宗商品（commodity）出口经济体。如果过去六个月大宗商品价格上涨，他们在出口石油、出口大豆。某种意义上，他们反而从伊朗战争中获益了。当然，加勒比地区和中美洲受创很重。而巴西的净影响其实大致扯平。这可能反倒帮了 Lula，尽管要真正看清数据、搞明白这一点，还需要很长时间。

turns.en: Should we talk Venezuela?
turns.zh: 我们要不要聊聊委内瑞拉？

turns.en: Yeah, yeah. All right.
turns.zh: 好啊，好啊。行。

turns.en: So going over to Venezuela, we have Machado who's come back. And now people are talking a little bit, a tiny bit about the potential to have elections over there. And I saw on Polymarket there's like an 8% chance being priced.
turns.zh: 那么转到委内瑞拉，Machado 已经回来了。现在人们开始稍微、那么一丁点儿地谈论那边举行选举的可能性。我在 Polymarket 上看到，给出的概率大概是 8%。

turns.en: Of an election.
turns.zh: 举行选举的概率。

turns.en: Of an election by the end of the year, which is fairly soon now. It's November. That's true. You're a super forecaster. What number would you put on it?
turns.zh: 在年底前举行选举的概率——而现在离年底已经挺近了，都 11 月了。这倒是真的。你是超级预测者（super forecaster）。你会给它一个什么数字？

turns.en: This year, there's not going to be an election. There's really going to be, there's about a six to nine month run up for any election that has to happen because there are steps that must occur. And now I worry about those steps being drawn out over years and years and years where they just keep kicking the can down the road. But it should be about a six month timeframe, right? So the current Rubio plan as it exists, I say Rubio, not Trump very specifically, the current Rubio plan is that Delcy Rodriguez will declare a vacancy in the presidency. There will be a new electoral board. And six months later, there will be elections. Elections would ideally happen in July of next year, but maybe they get pushed to September or November of next year. I think that's the ideal. What would Delcy Rodriguez like? Probably closer to 2028 or 2029. And so this is the fight that's going on, I think, right now inside between Rubio and the Venezuelan authorities and inside the U.S. government between Rubio and other aspects of the Trump administration. Because I do think that there are people within the Trump administration who would like to see that election delayed. But I know that Rubio wants it on his record, that Venezuelan democracy happened on his watch. And so he will be pushing hard, I think, for elections in the coming year.
turns.zh: 今年是不会举行选举的。任何一场必须举行的选举，都会有大约六到九个月的筹备期，因为有一些步骤是必须要走的。而现在我担心的是，这些步骤会被拖上一年又一年又一年，他们就这么不停地把问题往后踢（kicking the can down the road）。但这应该是六个月左右的时间框架，对吧？那么目前的 Rubio 方案——我特意说是 Rubio，而不是 Trump——目前的 Rubio 方案是：Delcy Rodriguez 将宣布总统职位空缺，会成立一个新的选举委员会（electoral board），六个月之后举行选举。理想情况下，选举会在明年 7 月举行，但也可能被推迟到明年 9 月或 11 月。我觉得那是理想情形。那 Delcy Rodriguez 会希望怎样呢？大概会拖到更接近 2028 或 2029 年。所以我认为，眼下正在进行的这场博弈，一方面是在 Rubio 和委内瑞拉当局之间，另一方面是在美国政府内部——Rubio 和 Trump 政府的其他部分之间。因为我确实认为，Trump 政府内部有人希望看到这场选举被推迟。但我知道 Rubio 想把这件事记在自己的政绩上——委内瑞拉的民主是在他任内实现的。所以我认为，在接下来的一年里，他会大力推动选举。

turns.en: So one of the things that I read in your newsletter, which I hadn't clicked is that or hadn't really thought of before, is that there had been a lot of criticism in Brazil and around the world towards Lula. For having been too friendly with Maduro. But you sort of flip the sides again. It's like, all right, Delcy, part of Maduro's party, kind of chummy with Trump. Maybe that allows Lula to create some space, maybe becomes an advocate for some sort of version of Venezuelan democracy. Talk to us about that link.
turns.zh: 我在你的 newsletter 里读到一件事，是我之前没反应过来、也没真正想过的：在巴西和世界各地，一直有很多针对 Lula 的批评，说他对 Maduro 太过友好。但你又一次把两边调了个个儿。变成这样：好，Delcy 是 Maduro 那个党的人，却跟 Trump 有点称兄道弟。也许这反倒让 Lula 能腾出一些空间，甚至成为某种版本委内瑞拉民主的倡导者。跟我们讲讲这其中的关联吧。

turns.en: So there's an element in which Lula has called for new elections in Venezuela, and he was way too friendly with Hugo Chavez and Nicolas Maduro and various other left-wing dictators across the hemisphere. He has been for much of his career. He can't be happy with how things are going in Venezuela, right? South America is Brazil's sphere of influence. And right now, Trump is treating Venezuela like a proxy colony in some ways. And so I think that Lula would like to see Some sort of independence by Venezuela from the U.S.
turns.zh: 这里有一点是，Lula 一直呼吁在委内瑞拉举行新的选举，而他对 Hugo Chavez、Nicolas Maduro 以及这个半球上其他各种左翼独裁者都太过友好——在他职业生涯的大部分时间里都是如此。他不可能对委内瑞拉目前的局面感到满意，对吧？南美洲是巴西的势力范围（sphere of influence）。而现在，Trump 在某种意义上把委内瑞拉当成了一个代理殖民地（proxy colony）来对待。所以我认为，Lula 会希望看到委内瑞拉在某种程度上摆脱美国的独立。

turns.en: Authorities.
turns.zh: 美国当局的（控制）。

turns.en: And he thinks that a new election would potentially benefit him in that way, whether or not that election goes left or center. That said, the Venezuelan opposition hates Lula. They blamed Lula for a lot of what went wrong, the reason that they were not able to get a transition over the years. And so it's unlikely you'd see a Machado-Lula hug fest and that they get along. But they could become quiet allies of each other in this quest to push Venezuela towards elections.
turns.zh: 他认为，一场新的选举可能会在这方面对他有利，不管这场选举是偏左还是偏中间。话虽如此，委内瑞拉的反对派痛恨 Lula。他们把很多出问题的地方都归咎于 Lula——归咎于这些年来他们一直无法实现政权过渡。所以你不太可能看到 Machado 和 Lula 抱成一团、亲密无间。但在这条推动委内瑞拉走向选举的路上，他们有可能成为彼此低调的盟友。

turns.en: Wait, can you just explain what influence exactly Brazil has over Venezuela or what leverage they actually exert here?
turns.zh: 等等，你能不能解释一下，巴西究竟对委内瑞拉有多大的影响力，或者说他们在这里到底能施加什么样的筹码（leverage）？

turns.en: That's a great question. So Lula... Brazil is Latin America's largest economy. It shares a border with Venezuela. Hypothetically, for years under Chavez and Maduro, there were tens of millions of development contracts that went from Brazil to Venezuela. And Brazil's construction companies constructed a bunch of Venezuelan infrastructure. Brazil should be influential in Venezuela. The fact that they haven't been is the surprise. They are the biggest military in South America. They're the biggest neighbor for Venezuela. They're the largest economy. They should be the most influential player in South America in Venezuela. But under Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil stepped back from a lot of the diplomatic efforts to push transition. And then under Lula, they did very little after Maduro stole the 2024 election. Both the right and the left in Brazil have taken that step back from what should be influence in South America. And I think Lula may want to reassert it because as presidents late in their second term often do, when they become lame ducks, they turn towards foreign policy because it's where they have the influence.
turns.zh: 这是个很好的问题。Lula……巴西是拉美最大的经济体，跟委内瑞拉接壤。按理说，在 Chavez 和 Maduro 执政的那些年里，有数千万计的发展合同从巴西流向委内瑞拉，巴西的建筑公司也承建了一大批委内瑞拉的基础设施。巴西本该在委内瑞拉很有影响力。而它一直没有，这才是让人意外的地方。巴西是南美洲军事力量最强的国家，是委内瑞拉最大的邻国，也是最大的经济体。它本该是南美洲在委内瑞拉问题上最有影响力的玩家。但在 Jair Bolsonaro 执政期间，巴西从很多推动政权过渡的外交努力中抽身退了出来。而在 Lula 治下，在 Maduro 窃取了 2024 年选举之后，他们几乎没做什么。巴西的右派和左派都从这种本该属于他们在南美洲的影响力上后退了一步。我认为 Lula 可能想重新把它捡起来，因为就像处在第二任期尾声的总统们常做的那样——当他们变成'跛脚鸭'（lame ducks）时，他们会转向外交政策，因为那是他们还能施加影响的地方。

turns.en: Setting aside democracy and all that, what's happening with oil and the corporate money? And is there evidence of the oil majors, et cetera, actually looking at Venezuela as a real opportunity for growth? Or is the story still that all the talented petroleum engineers left a long time ago, the infrastructure isn't in place, it's still too uncertain, it's mostly noise? Where do you stand on that?
turns.zh: 先把民主那一套放一边，石油和企业资本（corporate money）那边现在是什么情况？有没有证据表明，那些石油巨头（oil majors）之类的，真的把委内瑞拉看作一个实实在在的增长机会？还是说，故事仍然是那样：所有有才华的石油工程师早就走光了，基础设施不到位，还是太不确定，基本上就是些噪音？在这件事上你怎么看？

turns.en: The oil majors are looking, but they're not jumping it. Chevron is in. Chevron was in before. Chevron will be in for the next 50 years. The rest of the oil majors, including Exxon and Conoco, who were kicked out under the Chavez era, they're interested. Venezuela is a sea of oil. It would be a great place to go. None of the larger firms want to go into Venezuela prior to some sort of certainty that their contracts will be respected. And so what you see instead are the NABAP, which is the company that Alejandro Betancourt currently runs, the companies that are going in are small. They're not quite wildcatters, but they are the sort of companies that aren't there for the long run. They're there for the quick deals. And I think that as we look for, you know, how is Venezuela going to recover? How is Venezuela going to rebuild? You're not going to rebuild with a company that has never done serious oil drilling elsewhere in the world. And so one of the reasons to push for democracy in Venezuela is the fact that you do not get the oil majors to come in until they have that rule of law certainty. And they know that a 10-year investment or a 30-year investment is going to be able to stick and not just change two years from now when the government changes.
turns.zh: 石油巨头们确实在观望，但他们并没有贸然冲进去。Chevron 已经进去了。Chevron 之前就在，未来 50 年也会一直在。其余的石油巨头，包括在 Chavez 时代被赶出去的 Exxon 和 Conoco，他们是有兴趣的。委内瑞拉是一片油海，会是个很棒的去向。但没有一家大公司愿意在'合同会得到尊重'这一点有某种确定性之前，就进入委内瑞拉。所以你看到的反而是——比如 NABAP，也就是 Alejandro Betancourt 目前在经营的那家公司——真正进去的都是些小公司。它们还算不上那种投机钻探者（wildcatters），但它们是那种不为长远打算的公司，只是冲着快进快出的买卖去的。我认为，当我们去思考——你知道——委内瑞拉要怎么复苏？委内瑞拉要怎么重建？你是没法靠一家从未在世界其他地方做过正经石油钻探的公司来重建的。所以推动委内瑞拉民主化的理由之一就是：除非这些石油巨头拥有那种法治（rule of law）上的确定性，否则你根本没法让他们进来。他们要知道，一笔 10 年或 30 年的投资能够稳定存在，而不是两年后政府一变就全变了。

turns.en: Speaking of rule of law, I mentioned that headline that came out just before we started recording this, but the New York Times reporting that the U.S. is in negotiations for a potential military presence in Venezuela. What does that actually mean?
turns.zh: 说到法治，我前面提到过那条就在我们开始录制之前爆出来的头条——New York Times 报道说，美国正在就可能在委内瑞拉设立军事存在进行谈判。这到底意味着什么？

turns.en: So as I understand it, it's a status of forces agreement, which doesn't necessarily mean a permanent military base or military presence. Instead, it would be an agreement for the U.S. military to be there to train, to operate, to provide support, and maybe to engage in certain operations. There was just an operation a couple of days ago against an ELN camp near the Columbia border. It looks like the U.S. assisted the Venezuelan military in that. The U.S. wants these agreements so that we have legal certainty for what happens to the U.S. soldiers when they are in country. And the Trump administration would like that deal signed so that we can feel more comfortable having U.S. military presence in the region. But it doesn't mean like a permanent base by any means. At least that's not how I read it. They could change that tomorrow. But how I read it today is just a basic agreement.
turns.zh: 据我理解，这是一份驻军地位协定（status of forces agreement），它并不一定意味着永久的军事基地或军事存在。相反，它会是一份协议，允许美军待在那里进行训练、行动、提供支持，也许还参与某些军事行动。就在几天前，有一次针对哥伦比亚（Colombia）边境附近一个 ELN 营地的行动。看起来美国在那次行动中协助了委内瑞拉军方。美国想要这类协议，是为了当美国士兵身处该国境内时，我们在'他们会遭遇什么'这一点上有法律上的确定性。而 Trump 政府希望把这份协议签下来，这样我们才能对该地区存在美军感到更安心。但这绝不意味着一个永久基地。至少这不是我的解读。他们明天就可能改变这一点。但就我今天的解读来看，这只是一份基础性的协议。

turns.en: What would happen if there were a free election held tomorrow in Venezuela?
turns.zh: 如果明天在委内瑞拉举行一场自由选举，会发生什么？

turns.en: Maria Karina Machado would win.
turns.zh: Maria Karina Machado 会赢。

turns.en: Unambiguously?
turns.zh: 毫无悬念？

turns.en: Yes. There's essentially no doubt that if you were to put Maria Karina Machado versus Delcy Rodriguez tomorrow in an election... Better than 90 percent, assuming everything was free and fair, Maria Karina Machado wins. And the odds go up the more you allow for Venezuelan expats to vote. That's just inside of Venezuela, which I think I think it's important to note. There are a lot of Venezuelans who have left the country. About a quarter of the population has left the country over the last.
turns.zh: 是的。基本上毫无疑问：如果明天让 Maria Karina Machado 对阵 Delcy Rodriguez 举行一场选举……在一切自由公正的前提下，Maria Karina Machado 获胜的概率超过 90%。而且你越是允许委内瑞拉的海外侨民投票，这个概率就越高。这还只是委内瑞拉国内的情况——我认为有必要指出这一点。有非常多的委内瑞拉人已经离开了这个国家。在过去这些年里，大约四分之一的人口都离开了这个国家。

turns.en: Were she to become president at some point in the next couple of years, what would be what would she do? Like what would substantively would be the change?
turns.zh: 如果她在未来几年里的某个时候当上总统，她会做什么？就是说，实质上的改变会是什么？

turns.en: Of course, there's a lot to be done in Venezuela. And so first off, she needs to consolidate her control with the military and the police. And this is, I think, a big reason why the Trump administration didn't go with her originally is they weren't sure that she would have the respect of the armed forces. And I'm not defending their policy, but that was the reason that they gave was that they knew that Delcy Rodriguez would have control of the military and they weren't sure Machado would. And so Machado has to show that she can control the security forces. Then she needs to Fix the economy. And the economy is a wreck. It's one of the biggest economic collapses in world history that we've seen in Venezuela. That includes fixing the currency. That includes getting new oil investments. That includes fixing the economy outside of the oil economy as well. There are other sectors that need to be fixed. And she needs to restore democracy. And that includes having multiple parties. It can't just be the chavistas and the opposition forever. There should be a wider range of democratic parties. And she needs to somehow restore the checks and balances, which means she probably loses the next election, or her party does. And that's a really hard thing to ask any politician to do, to set up a system, knowing that you may be creating the environment where your party loses because of how the political pendulum will work.
turns.zh: 当然，委内瑞拉有很多事要做。首先，她需要巩固自己对军队和警察的控制。我想，这也是 Trump 政府最初没有选择她的一大原因——他们不确定她能否得到武装部队的尊重。我并不是在为他们的政策辩护，但他们给出的理由是：他们知道 Delcy Rodriguez 能掌控军队，却不确定 Machado 能不能。所以 Machado 必须证明她能掌控安全部队。然后她需要修复经济。而这个经济已经是一片废墟。我们在委内瑞拉所见证的，是世界历史上最严重的经济崩溃之一。这包括修复货币，包括引进新的石油投资，也包括修复石油经济以外的经济——还有其他一些部门也需要修好。而且她需要恢复民主。这包括拥有多个政党。不能永远就只有 chavistas（查韦斯派）和反对派这两方。应该有更广泛的民主政党。她还需要以某种方式恢复制衡（checks and balances），而这意味着她——或者她的党——很可能在下一场选举中落败。这对任何政治人物来说都是非常难的要求：去搭建一套制度，明知你可能正在创造一个让自己的党因为政治钟摆如何运作而落败的环境。

turns.en: I know we implied in our intro that we weren't going to talk about the US elections, North American elections, but You're a super forecaster. We're recording this on November 3rd. I kind of feel like we have to ask for an actual number.
turns.zh: 我知道我们在开场时暗示过，不打算聊美国选举、北美选举，但你是超级预测者，而我们是在 11 月 3 日录这期。我总觉得我们必须问你要一个实际的数字。

turns.en: So the Democrats are going to take the House.
turns.zh: 民主党（Democrats）会拿下众议院（the House）。

turns.en: We're recording this at 2.59 p.m. November 3rd.
turns.zh: 我们是在 11 月 3 日下午 2 点 59 分录的这段。

turns.en: I am 96% certain the Democrats are going to take the House of Representatives. I feel very confident in talking about what it means for the Democrats to take the House of Representatives. The Senate is closer to a coin flip than Nate Silver, who you had on last week. That said, the possibility for a blue wave is definitely there, but it's not certain yet. So I can't make a call in the Senate, but I can definitely make a call in the House. It's going Democratic.
turns.zh: 我有 96% 的把握，民主党会拿下众议院（House of Representatives）。对于'民主党拿下众议院意味着什么'，我非常有信心去谈。至于参议院（Senate），那更接近五五开——比你们上周请来的 Nate Silver 说的还要接近。话虽如此，出现'蓝色浪潮'（blue wave）的可能性确实存在，但还不能确定。所以参议院我没法下判断，但众议院我绝对可以：它会归民主党。

turns.en: Last question. What else should we be looking for in Latin America for the coming months? Any other elections coming up or anything?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。在接下来几个月里，我们在拉美还应该关注些什么？还有其他即将举行的选举之类的吗？

turns.en: There are local elections in Ecuador. That sounds really boring. Mayor of Quito.
turns.zh: 厄瓜多尔（Ecuador）有地方选举。这听起来真的很无聊。基多（Quito）市长选举。

turns.en: We'll do an episode on the run-up or preview episode for the Mayor of Quito episode. That sounds fun.
turns.zh: 我们可以为'基多市长'这期做一期赛前预热或者前瞻节目。听起来挺有意思的。

turns.en: El Nino is hitting Ecuador right now. And Ecuador, two years ago, had a series of blackouts. And they just started having power outages right now, which is not good for local elections and how they're going to function in Ecuador. So we have local elections in Ecuador. And then next year we get elections in Guatemala and elections in Argentina. And everybody's going to be watching the run-ups to the elections in Argentina because the start of this most recent right-wing wave, if you want to call it that, was Javier Millet. And so whether Javier Millet can win re-election or Argentina goes towards a different path is going to start defining the next pendulum swing in Latin America.
turns.zh: 厄尔尼诺（El Nino）此刻正在袭击厄瓜多尔。而厄瓜多尔在两年前经历过一连串大停电（blackouts）。现在他们又开始出现停电了，这对厄瓜多尔的地方选举以及选举将如何进行都不是好事。所以厄瓜多尔有地方选举。然后明年，危地马拉（Guatemala）会有选举，阿根廷（Argentina）也会有选举。每个人都会盯着阿根廷选举的赛前进程，因为这最近一波右翼浪潮——如果你愿意这么叫的话——的起点，就是 Javier Milei。所以，Javier Milei 能否连任、还是阿根廷会走向另一条路，将开始定义拉美下一次钟摆的摆动方向。

turns.en: All right, James Bosworth, thank you so much for coming back on the podcast. Thanks for coming in studio. Really appreciate you taking your time.
turns.zh: 好的，James Bosworth，非常感谢你再次来到我们的播客。谢谢你专程到演播室来。真的很感激你抽出时间。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: That was fun. I really liked talking to James. It actually makes a lot of sense. The first round was an election about Lula. And then the second round was an election, a referendum on Bolsonaro.
turns.zh: 刚才聊得很开心。我真的很喜欢和 James 对谈。这其实很有道理。第一轮是一场关于 Lula 的选举，而第二轮则是一场关于 Bolsonaro 的选举、一场对 Bolsonaro 的公投。

turns.en: Everything makes sense in hindsight. No, no, I agree. It's still really surprising. The prediction markets got it so, so wrong.
turns.zh: 事后看什么都说得通。不不，我同意。但这仍然非常令人惊讶，预测市场错得离谱。

turns.en: No, and of course, that's James's story of how it got it wrong. But I kind of buy it as a sort of, what would explain the electorate to shift in a short period of time? It's like, oh, we don't like this Lula guy. It's time for someone new. And then it's like, oh, okay, a new guy wins. Oh, yeah, but Bolsonaro. And then the votes turn. It kind of makes sense to me.
turns.zh: 是的，当然，那是 James 对'它为什么错'的解释。但我挺信这套说法的，把它当作对'选民为什么会在短时间内转变'的一种解释：就像，哦，我们不喜欢 Lula 这个人，是时候换新人了。然后，哦，好，一个新人赢了第一轮。哦，对，可那是 Bolsonaro。于是选票就掉头了。这在我看来挺说得通的。

turns.en: Yeah. To me, the big question is like, what does this mean for the orange wave?
turns.zh: Yeah。对我来说，最大的问题是：这对'橙色浪潮'意味着什么？

turns.en: Yeah. Right.
turns.zh: Yeah。对。

turns.en: And I take James's point that you have to deal with Trump in one way or another if you're South America, because he finds a way to sort of insert himself into everything. But is that going to be political? Like, would aligning with him be as politically popular now as it used to be?
turns.zh: 我认同 James 的观点：如果你在南美洲，你就得以某种方式跟 Trump 打交道，因为他总能想办法把自己插进所有事情里。但这在政治上会怎样呢？就是说，跟他站在一起，现在还会像以前那样在政治上受欢迎吗？

turns.en: Yeah, I know. That's the question. Look, you know, at some point, actually, we should do an episode on super forecasting, which I don't know anything about. So it's always like a a super forecaster. What's your thing? Actually, don't even. That's a whole subculture of people who are really good at forecasting. So I'm never going to doubt a super forecaster. You know, it's like, hey, I'm not one. But I still find it hard to believe that there isn't a penalty in much of the world for being seen as too chummy with Trump at a time when Trump's war with Iran has driven up costs for everyone around the world. I think like the polling for Nigel Farage, for example, in the UK has been sliding because he's seen as been too Trump friendly, etc. So who knows what's going to happen there? It still makes you want. Yeah, like. Yes, in the meantime, you got to work with them, of course, and you have to take them seriously, etc. But from an electoral standpoint, I don't know. I find it implausible that anyone really wants to be too friendly with him going into an election.
turns.zh: Yeah，我知道。这就是问题所在。你看，其实找个时间我们应该做一期讲超级预测（super forecasting）的节目——这方面我一窍不通。所以每次都是那种'你是超级预测者啊，你的专长是啥？'算了，别问了。那是一整个由特别擅长预测的人组成的亚文化群体。所以我永远不会去质疑一个超级预测者。你知道，就像，嘿，我自己又不是。但我仍然很难相信，在 Trump 对伊朗的战争推高了全世界每个人成本的时候，世界上很多地方对被看作跟 Trump 太近乎这件事，不会有任何代价。比如说，我觉得英国 Nigel Farage 的民调一直在下滑，就是因为他被看作对 Trump 太友好，等等。所以谁知道那边会发生什么呢？这仍然让人……Yeah，就是……当然，在此期间，你得跟他们合作，也得当回事，等等。但从选举的角度看，我就不确定了。我很难相信，会有谁真的想在临近选举时跟他走得太近。

turns.en: Except maybe for Rodriguez.
turns.zh: 也许 Rodriguez 是个例外。

turns.en: Except maybe for Rodriguez.
turns.zh: 也许 Rodriguez 是个例外。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: It's all very strange.
turns.zh: 这一切都非常奇怪。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.zh: 我们就聊到这儿吧？
